name: By the Numbers
subject: Maths, numbers and measurement
tagline: Twenty questions on digits, shapes, odds and the measures we live by. No calculator needed. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.w: Six, from the Greek 'hex'. A pentagon has five, a heptagon seven and an octagon eight.
questions.more: Bees build hexagonal honeycomb because it is the shape that encloses the most space for the least wax; mathematicians only proved this 'honeycomb conjecture' in 1999. Snowflakes are six-sided because of the angles at which water molecules bond. The nuts on your bicycle are hexagonal so a spanner can grip from six angles.

questions.q: What is the value of pi to two decimal places?
questions.w: 3.14, the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter.
questions.more: Pi goes on forever without repeating; it has been computed to more than a hundred trillion digits, though NASA uses just fifteen for navigating spacecraft. Pi Day is 14 March, written 3/14 the American way, which is also Einstein's birthday. 2.71 is the start of e, and 1.62 the golden ratio.

questions.q: A dozen is twelve. How many is a baker's dozen?
questions.w: Thirteen. Medieval English bakers added a loaf so they could not be accused of short measure.
questions.more: The Assize of Bread and Ale of 1266 set harsh penalties, including the pillory, for underweight loaves, and bakers hedged with an extra one. A 'gross' is twelve dozen, 144, and a 'score' is twenty, as in Lincoln's 'four score and seven years ago'.

questions.w: M, from the Latin 'mille'. D is 500, C is 100 and L is 50.
questions.more: The Romans had no zero and no easy way to multiply, which is partly why their numerals survive mostly on clock faces, film copyright dates and Super Bowls. The year 1888 is the longest ever written in Roman numerals, MDCCCLXXXVIII, and 2026 is MMXXVI.

questions.q: How many degrees are there in a right angle?
questions.w: 90, a quarter of a full turn.
questions.more: The 360-degree circle comes from the Babylonians, who counted in sixties, perhaps because 360 is close to the days in a year and divides neatly by so many numbers. The angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees, which Euclid proved around 300 BC in the Elements, the most reprinted textbook in history.

o: A whole number greater than 1 divisible only by 1 and itself
A number that ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9
A number with exactly three factors
questions.w: A whole number above 1 with no divisors except 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and so on. Two is the only even prime.
questions.more: Euclid proved there are infinitely many. The largest known, found in 2024, has more than 41 million digits. Primes are the backbone of internet security: multiplying two huge primes is easy, but working back from the product to find them is so hard that your bank relies on it. Cicadas emerge every 13 or 17 years, prime cycles that dodge predators' rhythms.

questions.q: In a room of just 23 people, what is the chance that two of them share a birthday?
questions.w: About 50 per cent. With 57 people it is 99 per cent.
questions.more: This 'birthday paradox' feels wrong because people think of their own birthday matching someone else's, not of the 253 different pairs in the room. Hash functions in computer security are designed with the same maths in mind. In a World Cup squad of 23, roughly half the teams have a shared birthday.

questions.q: What is the square root of 144?
questions.more: The square root symbol dates to a German book of 1525 and may be a stylised letter r for 'radix', root. The square root of 2, about 1.414, was the first number proved to be irrational, impossible to write as a fraction; legend says the Pythagorean who revealed it was drowned for his trouble.

questions.q: In the famous Monty Hall problem you pick one of three doors, the host opens another to reveal a goat and offers a switch. What should you do?
o: Switch: it doubles your chance of the car to two in three
Stick: your first instinct is usually right
Switch: it raises your chance to one in two
questions.w: Switch. Your first pick had a one-in-three chance; the host's reveal, which is never random, concentrates the other two-thirds on the remaining door.
questions.more: When the columnist Marilyn vos Savant gave this answer in 1990 she received about 10,000 letters, nearly a thousand from PhDs, telling her she was wrong. Computer simulations and a later experiment with real doors and real pigeons, which learn to switch faster than humans, settled it. Monty Hall hosted the game show Let's Make a Deal.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in the bath on realising how to measure the volume of an irregular object?
questions.w: Archimedes of Syracuse, who had been asked whether the king's crown was pure gold.
questions.more: An object pushed into water displaces its own volume, so he could compare the crown's density with gold's. The story is told by Vitruvius two centuries later and may be embroidered. Archimedes also worked out pi to within a hundredth and was killed by a Roman soldier in 212 BC, supposedly while telling him not to disturb his circles.

questions.q: The metre was originally defined in 1793 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to where?
o: The Equator, along the meridian through Paris
questions.w: The Equator, measured along the meridian that runs through Paris.
questions.more: Two astronomers spent seven years surveying the arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona during the French Revolution, and were arrested as spies more than once. Their figure was slightly off because the Earth is not a perfect sphere, so the 'real' metre is about 0.2 millimetres short. Since 1983 the metre has been defined by the speed of light.
